headlines.title: Power restored to some Bay Area customers affected by PG&E shutoffs
headlines.description: A PG&E spokesperson said Friday afternoon that power has been restored to some, but not yet all, of the customers affected across five Bay Area counties by power shutoffs the utility company implemented starting Wednesday to prevent its equipment from sparking wildfires. PG&E had announced what it calls Public Safety Power Shutoffs for about 90,000 customers across 29 counties starting Wednesday evening due to dry and windy weather. The National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning for interior North Bay mountains that was in effect through 11 a.m. Friday because of elevated wildfire dangers due to low humidity and wind gusts of up to 60 mph at the highest peaks. Thousands of the affected customers were in five Bay Area counties — Alameda, Contra Costa, Napa, Solano and Sonoma. PG&E spokesperson Tamar Sarkissian said Alameda County had 4,720 customers affected, and 1,666 of those had power restored as of Friday afternoon. Contra Costa County had 1,607 customers and 458 of those restored, while Napa County had 2,915 customers affected and 323 restored so far. In Solano County, only 32 customers were affected and all of those have their power back on, while in Sonoma County, crews had restored power to 952 of the 2,0444 customers affected, according to Sarkissian. The power shutoffs are expected to last into Saturday, though milder weather is expected this weekend and into early next week. People can visit pge.com/pspsupdates to find out if their location is affected by the power shutoffs. PG&E has opened community resource centers in affected areas that offer restrooms, device charging, Wi-Fi, bottled water and snacks, and other supplies. A list of the centers by county can be found online. PG&E is also encouraging customers who may need additional support to contact 211, including those who rely on power for medical needs or who have a disability.

headlines.title: Valkyries fever ramps up in Bay Area ahead of WNBA Finals Game 1 at Ballhalla
headlines.description: Bay Area hoops will be in the national spotlight with the WNBA Finals tipping off Saturday at San Francisco’s Chase Center. The best-of-seven series features the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream both competing for each respective franchise’s first title. Both teams are known for being defensive juggernauts. Golden State’s deep playoff run has united the Bay Area, with fans attending Chase Center games expected to make “Ballhalla” a nightmare for the Dream. What were the results from Valkyries vs. Dream regular season games? The Valkyries swept the regular-season series against the Dream, winning two games at home and one on the road. Golden State recorded victories of 77-66 and 78-75 over Atlanta at Ballhalla in late June before beating the Dream 88-83 in the most recent meeting July 4. Golden State Valkyries Oct 15 WNBA Oct 12 WNBA Oct 12 Postseason experience Atlanta is looking for its first title, but have made three Finals trips ahead of this year’s series against Golden State. The Valkyries made history in their inaugural season last year by qualifying for the 2025 WNBA Playoffs as the No. 8 seed with a 23–21 regular-season. Who has home-court advantage in the WNBA Finals? The Valkyries have home court due to being the higher seed. Golden State will host Games 1 and 2 at Ballhalla, along with the potential Games 5 and 7. How to watch Valkyries vs. Dream in the WNBA Finals The series will air across NBC and USA Network. Games 1 and 4 will be on NBC Bay Area. All games can also be streamed on Peacock. Where to stream Valkyries vs. Dream WNBA Finals games live online In addition to Peacock, there are other platforms where the Finals can be streamed. NBC broadcasts can also be seen on NBC.com and the NBC app, while USA Network broadcasts are available to watch on USANetwork.com and the USA Network app. Valkyries vs. Dream WNBA Finals schedule Here’s the full Finals broadcast schedule: Game 1: Dream at Valkyries — Saturday, Oct. 17, 3:30 p.m. ET/12:30 p.m. PT, NBC and Peacock Game 2: Dream at Valkyries — Monday, Oct. 19, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 3: Valkyries at Dream — Wednesday, Oct. 21, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 4: Valkyries at Dream — Saturday, Oct. 24, 1 p.m. ET/10 a.m. PT, NBC and Peacock Game 5 (if necessary): Dream at Valkyries — Monday, Oct. 26, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 6 (if necessary): Valkyries at Dream — Thursday, Oct. 29, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network Game 7 (if necessary): Dream at Valkyries — Saturday, Oct. 31, 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT, Peacock and USA Network

headlines.title: Zombie shooter game based on San Francisco's Tenderloin causes controversy
headlines.description: The creator of a controversial zombie shooting game set in San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood has taken the game down following city leaders’ requests. The game, called “Tenderloin Night Shift,” invited players to indiscriminately shoot zombies in a neighborhood that resembles the actual area. The game includes signature images of the city, including Waymos and e-scooters. In the game, players were invited to “meet the locals” as the screen shows a person folded over, much like someone struggling with a fentanyl addiction. Mayor Daniel Lurie called it horrific. “There’s no accounting for taste or people’s terrible ideas. This is a bad one and we reject it. It doesn’t speak for San Francisco values,” Lurie said. Lurie has been touting the city’s noticeable recovery from pandemic issues, including open-air drug markets and a boom in homeless encampments, over the last two years. NBC Bay Area reached out to the creator of the video game for comment in an interview either on camera or by phone, but he declined. In his initial response, the creator said he based the video game on what he sees in the Tenderloin on his commute to and from work every day. Pierre-Louis Biojout, the founder of a startup called NanoCorp, says he rejects the suggestion that the game promotes violence against residents. He wrote in part, “It was not intended to depict shooting real people or to target a particular demographic or group.” Over the last few days, people have taken to social media to blast the game and his attempts to advertise it. Advocates for the unhoused and for people experiencing drug addiction have said he’s monetizing people’s suffering. Supervisor Bilal Mahmoud, who represents the Tenderloin, says Biojout’s video game comes from a pretentious and privileged point of view. “I would say that he represents a minority voice. On the very same day this started to blow up, I was working with other people in the entrepreneurial community to announce the investment in the Arts District to support arts and independent theater and revitalizing the Tenderloin corridor on Market,” he said. Biojout recently said he’s taken the game offline and its promotional materials. He says he’s also refunded al money to advertisers and made a personal donation to a local foundation that services the unhoused and people in addiction recovery.

headlines.title: Santa Clara University to offer free education to eligible low-income students
headlines.description: For millions of low-income families, sending a student to a private university is next to impossible. Santa Clara University says it has a plan to change that. Beginning next fall, any California applicant who is accepted into the South Bay university and whose family earns less than $150,000 a year will receive a free college education as part of the university’s recently expanded California Promise program. “As a Jesuit institution, the university has made a commitment to try to meet 100% of demonstrated need of students,” said Cindy Tirado, the university’s director of financial aid. In addition to qualifying for admittance, eligible families also have to possess assets worth less than $120,000. Final eligibility will be determined using the applicant’s Federal Student Aid application, known as FAFSA. “I think a lot of times people think private college isn’t unattainable,” Tirado said. “This would make it attainable for a lot of families that don’t see us as a possibility. It’s going to be able to get them access to an education that they never thought they could have.”

headlines.title: San Francisco's Ripley's Believe It or Not! to close in December
headlines.description: Ripley’s Believe It or Not! will close its Fisherman’s Wharf location in San Francisco on Dec. 1 after 60 years. The attraction opened on Feb. 2, 1967. Notable visitors included Michael Jackson, Joe DiMaggio and former San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown. “We’ve had nearly 60 unbelievable years at Fisherman’s Wharf, and we want these final weeks to be a celebration,” said Jim Pattison Jr., president of Ripley’s Believe It or Not! World Entertainment. “Whether you visited us as a kid, brought your own kids years later, or have somehow never made it through our doors, we hope you’ll come see us one more time.” To mark the end of its run, every Thursday leading up to the final day guests can experience Ripley’s Believe It or Not! for $19.67. Admission on closing day will return to original 1967 attraction prices at just $1.50 for adults and 75 cents for kids. Some of its strangest treasures are also going up for auction. Guests can bid on items such as Joe DiMaggio’s crutches, a chicken-wire portrait of Janis Joplin and toothpick replicas of the Golden Gate Bridge.

headlines.title: Man injured in shooting after vehicle collision in Menlo Park
headlines.description: A shooting in Menlo Park on Thursday night injured a 47-year-old man who had three children in his vehicle and had just gotten into a collision with the suspected shooter’s car, according to police. Menlo Park police responded at 8:39 p.m. to reports of gunfire in the area of Bay and Hedge roads, located near Flood Park. Officers arrived and found the man with a gunshot wound and three children between the ages of 8 and 14 in his car. None of the children were hurt and the man was taken to a hospital and is expected to survive, police said. Investigators learned that a non-injury collision had occurred and when the man exited his vehicle to exchange information, someone in the other vehicle shot him. The vehicle was only described as a “small white car” and police did not share any details about the suspected shooter. Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact Detective Marcial Barron-Villa at mbarron-villa@menlopark.gov or 650-847-7438.

headlines.title: Mail-in ballots stolen from Daly City post office
headlines.description: The U.S. Postal Service is investigating after vote-by-mail ballots for San Mateo County were stolen from a Daly City post office, the county’s Registration & Elections Division said Thursday. The Elections Division said it was notified Wednesday of the mail theft that reportedly included mail-in ballots. The number of ballots that were stolen is still unknown. The county is working with USPS to investigate. Voters who are concerned that their ballots may have been affected by the theft may request a replacement ballot online or in person at any vote center in the county. Online requests for a replacement ballot must be submitted by Oct. 27 to allow sufficient time for mailing. Voters are encouraged to look up the status of their mail-in ballots through the California Secretary of State’s free ballot tracking service, “Where’s My Ballot.” The platform notifies voters when their ballot is mailed, received, and processed by the county elections division. There are currently three vote centers open in the county. Additional centers will open on Saturday, Oct. 24 and Saturday, Oct. 31, bringing the total to 50 vote centers. For a list of vote centers and ballot drop off locations, go to smcacre.gov. Voters with questions about their ballot status can contact the elections division at registrar@smcacre.gov or 650-312-5222.

headlines.title: California Prop 37: Measure would establish new down payment assistance program
headlines.description: It’s no secret the cost of living in California is unaffordable for many, even middle-class earners. Proposition 37 on the November ballot promises to change that by helping would-be homebuyers struggling to save up for a down payment, but critics argue its approval could actually drive up prices. The measure would create a $25 billion fund through revenue bonds, meaning the state will raise the money by selling bonds to investors, so taxpayers wouldn’t be on the hook. It would only apply to new homes. “It’s basically a second mortgage allowing people up to 17% down payment assistance,” said Gustavo González with the Santa Clara County Association of Realtors. To be eligible, the buyer must have lived in California for at least a year, live in the purchased home, and earn less than 200% of the area’s median income. “For example, in very expensive parts of the state, like Santa Clara County, it could be a family of four making up to around $400,000 a year, could still qualify for this program,” political analyst Guy Marzorati said. “The argument around Prop 37 is even folks who are making a lot of money, it’s difficult for them to save up for that down payment.” Elections Sep 17 Decision 2026 Oct 2 Critics say Prop 37 doesn’t actually address the lack of affordable housing and could even drive up prices. “Under Proposition 37, it’s $25 billion, and that would basically be used to create a California state government mortgage lending program,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio said. “Basically, the California state government would become one of the largest mortgage brokers in the entire state. I don’t want government being more involved.” DeMaio also argues developers would be the ones who truly benefit and claims the measure would destabilize the housing system. “This is not the approach for affordable housing,” he said. Marzorati said it could all boil down to a partisan preference. “This measure was placed on the ballot by former state Sen. Bob Hertzberg, who is a Democrat, and on the opponent side we’ve seen a lot of Republicans and kind of conservative groups,” Marzorati said.

headlines.title: Who is Elizabeth Holmes and what did she do?
headlines.description: Elizabeth Holmes continues to be a pop culture fascination and cautionary tale of hubris among tech start-up founders. The former CEO of the health technology company is the subject of the new documentary, “You Can See Everything,” which hits theaters on Oct. 16. The trailer for the film went viral in September for its eerie interactions between Holmes and comedian Nathan Fielder as well as its depiction of Holmes’ family life with partner Billy Evans and their two young children. The film is just the latest project involving the saga of Holmes, which has previously spawned an HBO documentary and a scripted Hulu series. Here’s what to know about her story and the new film. Movies Sep 7 Crime and Courts Sep 24 Who is Elizabeth Holmes? Holmes dropped out of Stanford University at 19 years old in 2003 to start Theranos, a Silicon Valley company that promised to revolutionize healthcare. The company’s stated goal was to use technology to run hundreds of blood tests using only a simple pinprick of blood in a proprietary machine Theranos called the Edison. Holmes raised nearly $1 billion from several prominent investors, including Oracle founder Larry Ellison, media mogul Rupert Murdoch, and heirs of the Walton family that owns Walmart. By 2014, Theranos was valued at $9 billion. She became a darling of Silicon Valley, appearing on a 2014 cover of Forbes that billed her as the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire due to her 50% stake in Theranos. In 2015, she was named one of Time Magazine’s 100 most influential people. The company’s image began to unravel after a series of investigative articles by The Wall Street Journal in 2015 raised serious questions about whether the Theranos technology worked. The saga was also detailed in the 2018 book “Bad Blood” by WSJ journalist John Carreyrou. Theranos was using existing commercially available blood-analysis technology and repurposing it to run its blood tests, according to The Wall Street Journal. A former Theranos lab associate who became a whistleblower testified at Holmes’ trial that the Edison machines routinely failed quality control tests and that their results were about as accurate as “flipping a coin,” according to CNBC. An investigation into the company resulted in the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing civil fraud charges against Theranos, Holmes and former president Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani. What did Elizabeth Holmes get convicted of? In January 2022, Holmes was convicted by a jury in a California court of four federal charges of wire fraud for misrepresenting to investors what the Theranos technology could do and how widely its Edison machines were being adopted. Prosecutors alleged that she duped investors into pouring money into a product she knew was faulty. Holmes denied the accusation during the trial. “At the time, you were not worried people would be given an inaccurate impression?” Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Leach asked her during the trial. “I was not,” Holmes said. Holmes was acquitted of charges of defrauding patients and one count of conspiracy. In May 2023, U.S. District Judge Edward Davila ordered her to pay $452 million in restitution to the victims of her crimes. Is Elizabeth Holmes still in prison? Yes, Holmes was sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in federal prison in November 2022. Balwani was sentenced to nearly 13 years in prison and three years of probation after being convicted of 12 counts of fraud. Holmes, 42, has been serving her sentence at a minimum-security prison in Bryan, Texas, but she is expected to be let out of prison into a halfway house. She is scheduled to be transferred to a halfway house next year, according to one of her victims. Alan Eisenman, who invested about $1.2 million in Theranos, told NBC News on Sept. 24 that he was notified that she is to be transferred to the Austin Transitional Center in an unincorporated community that borders Austin, Texas. The Department of Justice is required by law to notify victims of crime of case developments through letters and emails. Her scheduled release date is Feb. 22, 2030, after some reductions in her sentence. What makes the new movie different from previous projects? “You Can See Everything” is the latest film involving Holmes, and the most intimate. Amanda Seyfried won an Emmy for outstanding lead actress for her portrayal of Holmes in the 2022 scripted series “The Dropout” on Hulu. Holmes was also the subject of the 2019 HBO documentary “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.” In “You Can See Everything,” Holmes grants comedian Nathan Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim extraordinary access to her life in the months leading up to when she entered prison. She had a son with partner Billy Evans in 2021 and then gave birth to a daughter in 2023, shortly before she began serving her prison sentence. The documentary trailer shows Holmes maintaining that she did nothing wrong and reveals that Fielder moved into her home while filming. “I think this is the moment in time to capture this story before I’m gone,” she seemingly tells the comedian at one point. Evans also appears in the documentary and answers questions about his life with Holmes. There are also uncomfortable moments between Fielder and Holmes, including one in which he muses about whether he can trust her. “That’s because I don’t have anything to hide,” she tells him. This story first appeared on TODAY.com. More from TODAY: Hilary Swank, 52, Addresses Backlash Over Having a Baby Later in Life Baby Name Consultant Shares 1 Classic Baby Girl Name Nobody is Using — But Should What to Know About ‘Breaking Bad’ Actor RJ Mitte’s Cause of Death and Cerebral Palsy Diagnosis

headlines.title: Driver says he was asleep when Tesla crashed into CHP patrol car on I-80
headlines.description: Two California Highway Patrol officers are recovering after a Tesla hit one of their parked patrol cars on Interstate 80 in Fairfield earlier this week. CHP posted video online showing the crash, which happened Tuesday night west of Air Base Parkway. The officers were responding to a deadly crash when the Tesla drove through the crash site and hit the parked patrol car. The driver claimed he was asleep while using driver-assistance technology. It is unknown whether the Tesla’s Full Self-Driving feature was active at the time of the collision.

headlines.title: Authorities remove 44 dogs from Vallejo woman with previous animal cruelty conviction
headlines.description: Solano County sheriff’s deputies and animal control officers on Thursday removed 44 dogs from the home of a Vallejo woman who has previously been convicted of animal cruelty. The raid, authorized by a search warrant as part of an animal cruelty investigation into resident Susan Anthony, took place at a residence on the 800 block of Carolina Street in central Vallejo. “It’s a lot of dogs, so it’s overwhelming the shelter system,” said Sgt. Rex Hawkins from the Solano County Sheriff’s Office. “Dogs are being taken everywhere.” Hawkins did not comment on the health of the canines or the conditions they were living in, but said that a veterinary assessment of the canines is pending. Anthony runs California Carolina Dogs, a dog breeding and adoption business. She has kept and bred Carolina dogs, also known as American dingos, at several Vallejo properties for around 20 years, she said. Since 2013, neighbors and animal rights groups have lodged complaints against Anthony for operating a “puppy mill.” In May, Anthony was found guilty in Solano County Court on one count of animal cruelty for allegedly keeping and breeding a pack of dogs that ran wild on a small ranch in east Vallejo. According to court records, she was granted probation in June. On August 2023, a dog owned by Anthony was attacked so badly it had to be euthanized. In 2024, a puppy was killed by several dogs, and in one week, the pack twice attacked two of Anthony’s other dogs. Anthony is also in the midst of a civil suit brought by Caru Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals alleging that her organization’s practices are animal cruelty. She is scheduled to appear in court for a hearing in the case on Friday at Solano County Superior Court in Fairfield. Anthony, who was present during Thursday’s raid, maintained that the dogs are healthy and live a good life on the property, which sits on two lots in a residential area of Vallejo. Anthony said the raid was traumatic for the dogs, some of which yelped as they were caught and put into kennels. She said the dogs belong to her 99-year-old mother, who lives on Carolina Street. Anthony has vigorously defended her dog operation. In September 2025, she filed a motion for a restraining order against the county Animal Control, which was denied.

headlines.title: Natalie Nakase's high-energy, hands-on coaching has guided Golden State Valkyries to WNBA Finals
headlines.description: Natalie Nakase throws her arms up to guard Gabby Williams one moment, then moves to defend Veronica Burton the next as Golden State’s high-octane coach gets into it to help the Valkyries gear up for the WNBA Finals. She briefly steps out of the action to observe before jumping right back in to take a turn against Tiffany Hayes. And you bet Nakase can trash talk with the best of them. “Oh, yeah, I say, ‘Yeahhh!’ I say, ‘Not here! Not this time!,” she shared Wednesday. “I let them know. Because that’s effort. Again, it goes back to you can control that. I’m 46 years old, why am I getting that (stop)?” Nakase never stops moving, and it’s why everyone around her is offering regular reminders that she needs to eat for energy and rest just the way she stresses those things to her players. The coach collapsed on the court late in the deciding game of the first round with Dallas and later called it “a wakeup call” to prioritize her well being. Her players love and appreciate how hands-on she is with practices and game planning. “It probably brings back some memories of her being in uniform when she used to play,” Hayes said. “It’s definitely fun, but it’s more fun when we actually get the bucket on it ‘cause if she gets the stop we won’t hear the end of it.” That intensity and drive is something Hayes has seen for years, dating to their days when Nakase was an assistant with the Las Vegas Aces coaching Hayes and the guards. And it played a key role in Hayes following her to the Bay Area. Nakase had just been hired for her first head coaching job when she asked Hayes to take a chance on a brand new team and join her in San Francisco and start something special with the expansion Valkyries. Hayes had absolutely no reservations and the answer was a resounding yes. Her unfamiliarity with the Bay Area hardly mattered, because she had Nakase –- and that’s a sentiment many of Golden State’s players feel given how much she has invested in each one of them. Nakase has built a culture with the Valkyries in such a short time largely by finding a way to know each woman on a deeper level, far beyond just basketball. WNBA 9 hours ago WNBA Oct 12 She is breaking barriers With the Valkyries and their famous, violet-colored “Ballhalla” fan base on the big postseason stage, everybody is getting a glimpse of what Nakase vowed to do from Day 1: put Golden State on the map for women’s basketball after all those special NBA championship runs by Stephen Curry, Steve Kerr and the Warriors. And, no, she’s not surprised by the playoff success so soon — she thought the Valkyries should have made a run last year, when they lost in the first round to Minnesota after becoming the first expansion franchise to reach the postseason in its inaugural year. Nakase was groomed by some greats: Clippers coach Tyronn Lue, former Los Angeles assistant Armond Hill, who has been attending practice in Oakland this week, and Aces coach Becky Hammon. “You just celebrate people that are blowing away ceilings for women in sports, specifically women’s basketball, and obviously we’re a little biased toward Natalie,” UCLA coach Cori Close said of Nakase, the former Bruins guard. “I just think about what she’s done. She came to UCLA as a walk-on, then earned a scholarship, then became a captain, then was one of the first women hired on an NBA team and 10 years with the Clippers and really doing a great job with Becky Hammon and winning championships there. And now coming here and they say, ‘We want to win it in the first five years,’ and she’s like, ‘Bring it on, that’s exactly the kind of organization I want to be a part of,’ and then go back it up and then sell out every game. The list just goes on and on.” Nakase has found a way to relate to all of her players, and she works at it. Whether it’s learning about their culture or language, favorite music or dance move, she makes an effort to know everyone on her team far beyond just basketball. “I think my identity changes from year to year because I’m a constant learner,” she said. Uplifting the group does wonders Celebrating in the locker room after winning on Las Vegas’ home floor last Friday, Nakase praised her team for its fight in overtime to eliminate the defending champion Aces. She pointed to Kiah Stokes for making a key block, and teammates broke into chants of “Ki-ah! Ki-ah!” Then it was Kayla Thornton’s turn to be shouted out, for her rebounding. And cheers of “K-T, K-T!” The coach finished by acknowledging her two clutch finishers in crunch time, “the closers, you two,” and pointed at Hayes and Williams. Players started hollering “Tip! Tip! Tip!” and “Gab-by! Gab-by!” The Valkyries rallied from an 11-point deficit to pull off an 87-77 overtime victory in Las Vegas for an improbable sweep in the best-of-five WNBA semifinals. “Down 11 meant nothing, right? You guys stayed connected, you guys stayed composed. What I loved was your fight, everyone brought another level of fight,” Nakase told them. “It was pure joy.” Success has affected her health But this special season hasn’t come without challenges for Nakase. She scared her family and everybody else when she went down in the closing minutes of the clinching Game 3 against the Wings earlier this month. Yet the coach got back up and finished the final 1:40. When Nakase saw her sister in tears afterward, she realized she had to take better care of herself to be there for others. She leaned more on her assistants. “You could want to win as much as you want but if my tank is not full, whether it’s rest, food, hydration, everything, then I’m not going to be able to give my full self during the game as you guys saw,” she said. “It’s doing that.” Nakase’s late father, Gary, influenced most everything she does. She watched him overdo it at times. Her former players are accustomed to how hard Nakase pushes herself. “That’s Natalie and that’s about giving her all, literally 100%,” Aces center A’ja Wilson said. “She’s a warrior, it’s what she does. She eats, sleeps, breathes basketball.” Valkyries owner Joe Lacob could see it when he interviewed Nakase over a late breakfast in Las Vegas two years ago. “She’s everything I thought she would be,” Lacob said. “I’m so happy for her, she continues to impress me with her coaching, she’s just terrific.” While handling video duties as an intern for the Clippers, Hill asked what her goal was and Nakase told him she wanted to be a head coach one day. He replied, “OK, let’s get to it.” “He’s the reason why I’m here, seriously,” she said. “… He calls me grasshopper, because I’m always anxious, I want to do everything right, I’m a perfectionist, I’m an extremist but he’s all about, ‘Hey, just take a breath, make sure you’re clear and concise with your game plan, try not to get everything done all in one night and more importantly take care of your health.’” She honors her late father every day in all she does, committed to treating the job as a tremendous opportunity. “I’m always going to be a fighter,” Nakase said. “That’s how my dad raised me.” ___ See AP’s full WNBA coverage here
